title: RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses
authors: Peng Xia, Rujun Han, Zifeng Wang, Yanfei Chen, Yufan Zhuang, Yoonho Lee, Chengsong Huang, Han Yu, Zhongying CuiZhu, Yifei Ming, Huaxiu Yao, Burak Gokturk, Tomas Pfister, Chen-Yu Lee
lab: Google Cloud AI Research, with Stanford University (Yoonho Lee), Washington University in St. Louis (Chengsong Huang) and UNC-Chapel Hill (Huaxiu Yao); Peng Xia as a Student Researcher at Google Cloud AI Research
date: Submitted 21 September 2026 (v1), revised 23 September 2026 (v2, which corrects one author's name and is the version this page links)

code.title: google-research/rrsi, Apache-2.0
code.note: The search loop for all three instances (coding, workspace, engineering), each instance's starting harness, prompts and hyperparameter file, with a quickstart. The four baselines are not in it, and neither are the evaluation infrastructures (harbor, Harvey LAB, EngDesign are separate checkouts)

site.label: project page with the released run records

takeaway: Regularising recursive harness evolution with an annealed edit budget, a critic and a pruner buys +14.1 points in distribution, +4.7 out of distribution and 30% fewer policy tokens, which is the first evidence the loop's gains survive leaving the benchmark it was scored on.
takeaway_note: the +14.1 is the gain on the split the search was scored on, with a secondary policy (Gemini 3.5 Flash; with the main policy the evolve gains are 6.0, 1.1 and 4.9); +4.7 is the best of five out-of-distribution gains, not their sum or mean (the mean is 3.6); and the paper's own Table 2 gives 36% fewer tokens, not 30%. Concurrent work also measures generalisation, so "first" is too strong. {{Details|tab:t-read:s-trust}}.
verdict: Believe the diagnosis, and that RRSI's rules run as described: the authors' released run records replay to the same decisions. Treat the transfer gains as plausible but unproven: every arm is a single run, each out-of-distribution gain is within about one standard error, most edits the runs kept were inside their own noise band, and the released held-out record shows +0.9 points where the paper prints +2.3.

headline.d: 43.6 against 39.7 for the unevolved harness; unregularised evolution +0.6

headline.k: on each of the five out-of-distribution benchmarks
headline.d: no held-out split regresses; each gain alone is within about one standard error
36% fewer (the abstract says 30%); the unevolved harness uses 1.56M

resources.t: Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse
resources.by: Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold, Roth (2015)
resources.n: The theory behind the paper's worry: every look at the same evaluation set adapts the next choice to it, so scores on a reused set drift above the truth. Its reusable-holdout idea is the formal cousin of RRSI's noise band.

resources.t: What Evolves When We Talk About Harness Evolution?
resources.by: Ding, Lu, Yu, Li, Jin, Liu, Durrett (2026)
resources.n: Delta attribution: separates edits that install a reusable mechanism from edits that fit the evolution tasks; the paper cites it as evidence that evolution gains often do not transfer.
Concurrent work that makes generalisation an explicit objective of harness evolution, the alternative to RRSI's regularise-the-search approach.
One of the four baselines: an observability-driven evolution loop for coding-agent harnesses; here it reaches 90.7 on the evolve split and ends below the starting harness out of distribution.
Baseline: a harness built from typed, composable primitives with trace-driven adaptation.
Baseline: keeps several candidate harnesses and lets an agentic judge pick the one that persists; the largest out-of-distribution drop in Table 1.

kb.t: SoL-Pi: Recursively Scaling Auto-Research Loops for Efficient Agent Harness
kb.n: The same harness-level loop pointed at cost instead of capability: about half of recorded agent token traffic turns out to be harness overhead. RRSI's cost rule is the guard; SoL-Pi is the objective.

kb.t: Dream-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Worlds
kb.n: Keeps the loop's memory as a replayable search history and improves exploration off-policy against it; RRSI keeps an edit ledger and conditions the proposer on it. Neither measures transfer to new benchmarks the way RRSI tries to.

kb.t: Agora: Git as Shared Memory for Collective AutoResearch
kb.n: Memory as an append-only Git history that anyone can check out; RRSI's released code also makes every incumbent a commit on an evolve branch.

kb.t: NeoHorse-1: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement via Agentic Post-Training with Routing Harness
kb.n: Recursive self-improvement through the weights: the harness feeds a training curriculum. RRSI freezes the weights and changes only the harness, and its Limitations section names weight updates as out of scope.

kb.t: HarnessDev: Can LLMs Create and Evolve Their Own Agent Harness?
kb.n: Measures the failure RRSI tries to prevent: in its evolution runs the score a creator could see moved with the held-out score in only 34 of 64 version changes.

kb.t: Emergence World: Adversarial Stress-Testing of Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Systems
kb.n: Attacks long-running agent systems of this shape with prompt injection, misinformation and memory exposure; a self-modifying harness is exactly the kind of system it stress-tests.

kb.t: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
kb.n: A harness that versions its own prompts and skills across trajectories: an unregularised loop of the kind RRSI regularises.

kb.t: JIT-Agent: Scaling Harness Intelligence via Just-in-Time Harness Evolution
kb.n: Evolves a harness per task at inference time instead of searching one shared harness offline.

topics.n: Where this paper is integrated: the harness-scaling and self-improving-harness thread.
The regularisation analogies (L0, L1, L2, entropy) come from training; here they act on a search over programs.
Eight benchmarks, three of them graded by LLM judges; the evolve/held-out/out-of-distribution split is the paper's contribution to how such loops should be reported.
